# Ink and Empire: Missionary Printing Presses in Late Qing Guangzhou

The arrival of movable metal type in Guangzhou in the 1840s marked a pivotal moment in the history of Chinese print culture, a testament to the transformative power of technology.¹ Yet the story is not simply one of Western innovation diffusing outward; it is also one of local printers who adapted, resisted, and ultimately reshaped these tools.²

As Cynthia Brokaw has shown, woodblock printing remained economically dominant well into the 1880s.³ The missionary presses — never more than a handful — produced perhaps 2 percent of the city's printed output by volume, though estimates vary widely.⁴ Their significance lay elsewhere: in typography, in the standardization of certain characters, and in the commercial networks they seeded.

It could be argued that the missionaries' greatest legacy was unintended. Several Chinese compositors trained at the London Missionary Society press later founded independent shops; at least one, Huang Sheng, went on to co-found a Hong Kong newspaper in 1874.⁵
